case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, when a copyright claim is timely under the discovery-accrual rule, 17 U.S.C. § 507(b) nonetheless bars the plaintiff from recovering monetary relief for infringements that occurred more than three years before the complaint was filed.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 17 U.S.C. § 507(b) (Copyright Act statute of limitations: “No civil action shall be maintained ... unless it is commenced within three years after the claim accrued.”)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Warner Chappell Music and Artist Publishing Group) argue that even if a claim is considered timely under a discovery-based accrual rule, § 507(b) imposes a separate, absolute three-year lookback cap on retrospective monetary recovery—so damages (and similar retrospective relief) cannot be awarded for infringing acts occurring more than three years before suit. They contend this reading is compelled by the structure and purpose of limitations law, is consistent with the Supreme Court’s discussion in Petrella v. MGM, and avoids effectively creating open-ended damages exposure whenever a plaintiff plausibly pleads late discovery. They emphasize administrability, evidentiary staleness, and business reliance interests, and warn that the Eleventh Circuit’s approach would undermine repose by allowing decades-old damages based on delayed discovery.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Nealy and Music Specialist) argue that § 507(b) contains a single limitations requirement—file within three years after the claim “accrued”—and once a claim is timely under the governing accrual rule (including discovery accrual as applied by most circuits), the Copyright Act does not add an extra, categorical three-year damages bar. They read Petrella as addressing a different scenario (a concededly time-barred claim under injury accrual and a separate equitable-laches issue), and maintain that importing a hard damages lookback conflicts with discovery accrual’s function and would deny full remedies for timely claims, especially where infringement was concealed or not reasonably discoverable. In their view, ordinary doctrines (proof problems, equitable limits, willfulness standards, etc.) can address staleness without rewriting § 507(b).
key_precedents: Graham County Soil & Water Conservation Dist. v. U.S. ex rel. Wilson, 545 U.S. 409 (2005)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point for petitioner: Petrella’s repeated “three years back” phrasing and the repose function of short limitations periods. But Justice Barrett’s textual point remains decisive for me—§ 507(b) regulates when an “action” must be “commenced” after a claim “accrued,” and it nowhere imposes a separate remedial lookback once a suit is timely under the governing accrual rule; converting Petrella’s description of separate-accrual consequences into an independent damages cap adds a second, atextual time bar. Justice Alito’s Rotkiske/TRW citation strengthens caution about adopting discovery accrual in the first place, yet it does not supply affirmative authority to graft a remedies cutoff onto a timely action, and minimalism counsels we not decide the reserved accrual question indirectly through a damages rule. Repose concerns can be addressed through the accrual rule we adopt in a proper case and through existing doctrines, rather than by rewriting § 507(b)’s single limitations command.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice press the strongest textual objection—that § 507(b) speaks only to when an action must be “commenced” and does not expressly cap remedies—but that framing treats a limitations period as a mere filing instruction divorced from its historically understood function to limit the temporal reach of coercive relief. On the original public meaning, allowing discovery accrual to make decades-old infringements newly “accrued” and then awarding full retrospective damages would effectively nullify Congress’s three-year boundary; that is the more serious atextual move, because it drains the statute of its repose function. Justice Kagan’s attempt to confine Petrella’s repeated “retrospective relief only three years back” language to injury-based separate accrual is unpersuasive: Petrella described the operative consequence of § 507(b)’s limitations regime on backward-looking monetary relief, not mere dicta contingent on one accrual variant. Justice Alito is right that Rotkiske and TRW underscore the separation-of-powers problem with judge-made accrual doctrines that, in practice, defeat congressionally chosen temporal limits, supporting our reading that monetary recovery cannot reach beyond three years before suit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point that § 507(b) contains only one explicit command about when an action must be commenced and does not expressly speak in remedial terms, and I agree we should be wary of manufacturing extra-statutory rules. But I think Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right that Petrella’s repeated description of the statute’s operation—retrospective relief “only three years back”—is not empty narration; it reflects the ordinary repose function Congress chose in a short limitations period for discrete infringements, and it becomes incoherent if we pair discovery accrual with effectively unlimited backward monetary exposure. Rotkiske and TRW, while not about remedies, reinforce the separation-of-powers concern that judge-made accrual expansions should not, in practical effect, nullify Congress’s temporal boundary—so I would read § 507(b) to bar damages for infringements more than three years before suit even if the claim is timely under discovery. Justice Barrett’s ‘rewriting’ objection underestimates that the more aggressive judicial move is to accept discovery accrual and then deny the statute any meaningful constraint on retrospective liability, undermining the staleness and reliance interests the limitations period is designed to protect.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch make the strongest point that limitations periods traditionally serve repose and that Petrella repeatedly spoke in “three years back” terms, but that cannot substitute for statutory text: § 507(b) regulates when an “action” must be commenced, not how far damages may reach once a claim is timely under the governing accrual rule. As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize, turning Petrella’s description of injury-based separate accrual into a freestanding remedial cap would be a second, judge-made time bar that effectively decides the reserved discovery-accrual issue by indirection—especially punishing concealed infringement where less-resourced creators are least able to sue quickly. Rotkiske/TRW, raised by Justice Alito, may counsel skepticism about recognizing discovery accrual absent textual grounding, but they do not justify inventing an additional remedies limitation Congress did not enact; staleness and reliance concerns can be handled through evidentiary burdens and tailored remedies without rewriting § 507(b).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the best point for petitioner: Petrella’s “three years back” phrasing reflects the repose function limitations periods often serve, and they worry discovery accrual could otherwise expose defendants to very old damages. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 507(b) contains one textual instruction—suit must be commenced within three years after accrual—and it does not speak in remedial terms; turning Petrella’s descriptive account of separate-accrual consequences into an independent damages cap adds a second time bar Congress did not enact. Justice Alito’s reliance on Rotkiske/TRW usefully cautions against casually embracing discovery accrual, but those cases do not authorize importing an extra, atextual remedies cutoff once timeliness is satisfied under the governing accrual rule; staleness concerns can be handled through proof burdens and remedial tailoring rather than a categorical judicial lookback rule.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s best point is textual: § 507(b) speaks to when an action must be “commenced,” not to remedies, and she warns against turning Petrella into a silent remedial cap. But I think that framing misconceives petitioner’s position: the three-year limit on retrospective monetary relief follows from applying Congress’s three-year limitations judgment to backward-looking damages liability, not from grafting an extra, free-standing bar onto the statute. Justice Kagan’s effort to cabin Petrella’s “only three years back from suit” language to injury-based separate accrual gives too little weight to Petrella’s repeated description of the statute’s operative effect on retrospective relief, and it invites discovery accrual to do remedial work (unlocking decades-old damages) that the text does not clearly assign. Rotkiske/TRW, as Justice Alito notes, do not directly decide this remedies question, but they reinforce the separation-of-powers caution against judicial constructions of accrual that, in practice, erase the repose line Congress enacted.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan make the hardest point: § 507(b) is framed as a single filing deadline and does not expressly speak in remedial terms, so a categorical lookback can look like an extra, judge-made bar. But Petrella’s repeated “retrospective relief only three years back from the time of suit” language is difficult to reduce to mere narrative about separate accrual without destabilizing the administrable repose line Congress chose and this Court has already given operative content; in my institutionalist methodology, we should be reluctant to invite a regime where discovery accrual plus full retrospective damages effectively nullifies the practical constraint of a short limitations period. Justice Sotomayor’s proposal to rely on proof burdens and equitable tailoring is too variable to substitute for a clear, predictable temporal boundary that parties can rely on ex ante, especially given evidentiary decay and reliance interests. Rotkiske/TRW, as Justice Alito notes, doesn’t itself create a remedies cap, but it reinforces the separation-of-powers concern that courts should not use accrual doctrines to defeat Congress’s three-year limitations judgment in practice.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest opposing point: that limitations periods historically serve repose and that Petrella’s “three years back” language should be read as an operative remedial boundary. But under a textualist approach, § 507(b) imposes one condition—an action must be commenced within three years after the claim accrued—and it does not separately regulate the temporal scope of monetary recovery once a claim is timely; converting Petrella’s descriptive phrasing (in a separate-accrual posture) into a freestanding damages cap adds a second time bar Congress did not enact. Justice Alito’s invocation of TRW and Rotkiske rightly cautions against judge-made accrual rules untethered to text, yet those cases do not supply affirmative textual authority to graft an additional remedial limit onto timely claims after accrual is identified under the governing rule. Repose concerns are real, but they should be handled through the accrual doctrine itself and the Copyright Act’s existing remedial and evidentiary constraints, not by judicially rewriting § 507(b).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that limitations periods inherently do repose work and that Petrella’s “three years back from suit” phrasing reflects an operative remedial boundary—has policy force, but it still cannot supply statutory text that § 507(b) lacks. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, the statute imposes one temporal requirement keyed to when an “action” is “commenced” after a claim “accrued”; turning Petrella’s description of injury-based separate accrual into a freestanding damages cap would be a judicially added second time bar. Justice Alito’s Rotkiske/TRW caution about implying discovery accrual may matter in the distinct question whether discovery accrual exists, but it does not justify importing an extra remedial limitation once timeliness is satisfied under whatever accrual rule governs. On a pragmatic, fairness-oriented view, staleness and reliance concerns can be addressed through proof burdens and tailored equitable relief, without effectively gutting discovery accrual (and harming concealed-infringement plaintiffs) by indirection.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 507(b) sets a single limitations rule—an action must be “commenced within three years after the claim accrued”—and it does not separately cap remedies once a claim is timely under the governing accrual standard. Petrella v. MGM, 572 U.S. 663 (2014), addressed injury-accrual timeliness and laches, and its discussion of relief “limited to three years” is best read in that context rather than as creating an atextual damages lookback that would effectively decide (and substantially diminish) the still-unresolved discovery-accrual question. Imposing an additional categorical damages bar would rewrite § 507(b), conflict with the premise of discovery accrual (that the claim has not yet accrued), and risk unnecessary disruption of settled circuit practice—an institutional cost better avoided absent clearer statutory text. Staleness and reliance concerns can be managed through proof burdens and equitable limits without creating a new, judge-made remedial restriction not found in the statute.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 17 U.S.C. § 507(b) requires that an action be commenced within three years after the claim “accrued,” and a limitations period is ordinarily understood to restrict retrospective relief to prevent stale claims and preserve repose. Even assuming arguendo that a discovery-accrual rule can make a claim timely, Petrella v. MGM repeatedly described § 507(b) as “allowing plaintiffs to gain retrospective relief running only three years back from the date the complaint was filed,” which reflects the statute’s operative temporal limit on monetary recovery for past infringements. Reading § 507(b) to permit damages for infringements decades earlier whenever discovery is delayed effectively nullifies the statute’s three-year limitation and expands federal power beyond the enacted text. Consistent with textualism and the original public meaning of limitations statutes, § 507(b) bars monetary relief for infringing acts occurring more than three years before suit.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 507(b) provides that no civil action may be maintained unless commenced within three years after the claim accrued, and Petrella repeatedly explained that this limitations scheme "takes account of delay" by imposing a three-year limit on retrospective relief, making it inconsistent with open-ended damages exposure. Even assuming some form of discovery accrual, reading the statute to permit recovery for infringements decades in the past would undermine repose, exacerbate evidentiary staleness, and disrupt settled reliance interests—practical consequences Congress ordinarily addresses through firm limitations rules. Petrella reserved the validity of a broad discovery rule, and more recent cases like Rotkiske and TRW caution against judicially expanding discovery-based accrual absent clear statutory text, reinforcing a narrower construction that caps retrospective monetary relief to the three years preceding suit. Accordingly, a timely-filed action under any accrual rule does not authorize damages for infringing acts occurring more than three years before the complaint.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 507(b) contains a single timing command—an action must be commenced within three years after the claim “accrued”—and it does not textually impose an additional, categorical three-year cap on monetary recovery once a claim is timely under the governing accrual rule. Petitioners’ proposed “lookback” would functionally nullify discovery accrual in concealed or hard-to-detect infringement cases by allowing timely plaintiffs little or no meaningful relief, undermining the Copyright Act’s remedial scheme in §§ 504–505 and falling hardest on less-resourced rights-holders. Petrella v. MGM discussed a three-year lookback in the context of injury-based accrual and laches, while expressly leaving open whether discovery accrual applies; it should not be extended to create an extra-statutory damages bar for claims that are timely under discovery. Ordinary concerns about stale evidence and reliance can be addressed through proof burdens, equitable limits, and willfulness/innocent-infringer doctrines rather than rewriting § 507(b).

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 507(b) sets a single limitation: a civil action must be commenced within three years after the claim "accrued"; it does not separately cap remedies by imposing an additional three-year lookback once accrual is determined. Petitioners’ proposed damages bar effectively rewrites § 507(b) to add a second temporal limit Congress did not include, and it sits awkwardly with discovery accrual’s function of making a claim timely when the infringement was not reasonably discoverable. Petrella v. MGM addressed laches and the separate-accrual principle under an injury-based framework; its discussion that relief is ordinarily confined to the three years prior to suit does not establish an independent, across-the-board damages cap for timely claims under a different accrual rule. Workability and staleness concerns can be handled through proof burdens and equitable tailoring without creating atextual remedial limits inconsistent with § 507(b)’s structure.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 507(b) provides that no civil action may be maintained unless commenced within three years after the claim accrued, and limitations periods ordinarily carry with them a firm temporal boundary for retrospective monetary relief; reading “accrued” to allow discovery-based timeliness while still permitting decades of damages risks nullifying Congress’s repose judgment. Petrella v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer repeatedly described § 507(b) as allowing retrospective relief “only three years back from the time of suit,” and that understanding best harmonizes the statute’s text with the separation-of-powers principle that courts may not extend congressionally prescribed limits by judicially created accrual doctrines. Where ambiguity remains, the better course is administrable and faithful to the statute: timely suit under whatever accrual rule applies does not authorize recovery for infringements outside the three-year lookback. This reading also avoids effectively open-ended damages exposure based on contested “late discovery” assertions, a result Congress did not clearly command.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 507(b) provides that no civil action may be maintained unless commenced within three years after the claim accrued, and in Petrella v. MGM the Court repeatedly described that limitations scheme as permitting “retrospective relief only three years back from the time of suit,” a practical boundary that protects repose and mitigates evidentiary staleness. Even assuming a discovery-accrual rule governs timeliness, reading § 507(b) to allow damages for infringements indefinitely far back would substantially dilute the statute’s workability and undermine reliance interests—concerns Petrella emphasized in cabining stale claims and rejecting laches as an end-run around Congress’s chosen limits. Given the Court’s institutional interest in clear, administrable rules and the strong signals in Petrella about a three-year backward limit on monetary recovery, I would hold that damages are capped to the three years preceding suit notwithstanding discovery accrual.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 507(b) contains a single textual constraint: an action must be “commenced within three years after the claim accrued,” and it does not separately cap remedies by imposing an additional three-year damages “lookback” once accrual is determined under the governing rule. Petitioners’ proposed cap effectively rewrites § 507(b) to add a remedial limitation Congress did not enact; under a textualist approach, any such limit must come from the statute’s words, not general repose concerns. Petrella v. MGM addressed injury-accrual and rejected laches as a tool to curtail timely claims; its discussion of the “three-year lookback” describes the consequence of each discrete infringement’s own accrual, not an independent damages bar overriding a timely claim under a different accrual rule. And while Rotkiske v. Klemm and TRW Inc. v. Andrews caution against judicially creating discovery rules where Congress has not provided them, they do not support grafting an extra-statutory damages cap onto § 507(b) once timeliness is established under the applicable accrual doctrine.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 507(b) sets a single condition: an action must be “commenced within three years after the claim accrued,” and it does not separately cap remedies once a claim is timely under the governing accrual rule. Petitioners’ proposed three-year “damages lookback” adds a limitation Congress did not write and would undermine the practical function of discovery accrual—especially where infringement was not reasonably discoverable—by denying full monetary relief for a timely claim. Petrella v. MGM addressed laches and injury-based accrual for successive infringements, expressly reserving the discovery-rule question, and its statements about retrospective relief cannot be read to silently impose an additional damages bar for timely discovery-accrued claims. Consistent with procedural fairness and ordinary limits on stale proof, concerns about delay can be handled through evidentiary burdens and equitable discretion rather than rewriting § 507(b).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether, given the discovery-accrual rule for copyright claims, 17 U.S.C. § 507(b) bars a plaintiff from recovering monetary relief for infringements that occurred more than three years before the lawsuit was filed.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 17 U.S.C. § 507(b) (Copyright Act: civil actions must be “commenced within three years after the claim accrued”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that even if a claim is timely under a discovery-based accrual rule, § 507(b) still imposes a strict three-year backward limit on damages (and related retrospective monetary remedies), so a plaintiff may not recover for infringement acts occurring more than three years before filing suit; they contend this reading best fits the statute’s limitations function, promotes repose and evidentiary reliability, prevents open-ended liability where discovery is delayed, and aligns with how limitations periods ordinarily cap retrospective relief.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that under the widely used discovery-accrual rule, a claim does not “accrue” until the plaintiff discovers (or reasonably should discover) the infringement, and once the suit is filed within three years of that accrual, § 507(b) does not separately truncate damages to the last three years; instead, plaintiffs may recover for proven infringements that predate filing by more than three years so long as the action itself is timely under discovery accrual, with traditional equitable doctrines (laches-like considerations, equitable limits, prejudice, proof problems) and copyright-specific remedial rules supplying any needed constraint.
key_precedents: SCA Hygiene Products Aktiebolag v. First Quality Baby Products, LLC, 580 U.S. 328 (2017)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor fairly press the strongest point: § 507(b) is cast as a commencement rule and does not, in terms, speak in remedial language, so a categorical damages cap can sound like adding words. But Petrella’s repeated explanation—emphasized by Justice Alito—that the Act “takes account of delay” by limiting “retrospective relief only three years back” supplied the operative justification for rejecting laches, and that rationale collapses if discovery-based timeliness simultaneously allows essentially unlimited backward monetary exposure. Justice Thomas’s invocation of TRW and Rotkiske reinforces my minimalist separation-of-powers instinct not to treat statutory silence as license for expanding liability; assuming arguendo discovery for filing, the narrower, more administrable reconciliation is to preserve a three-year backward limit on monetary relief rather than resolve the broader accrual question. Justice Jackson’s proposed case-by-case tailoring and proof-burden approach is too indeterminate to substitute for the clear repose boundary Petrella understood the statute to provide, and it risks inconsistent, legitimacy-undermining adjudication.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that § 507(b) speaks to when an action must be “commenced,” not to remedies, so a three-year lookback sounds like an atextual damages cap. But that objection assumes a discovery-based understanding of “accrued”; on the ordinary public meaning, a claim accrues when the plaintiff has a complete cause of action—at the infringing act—so § 507(b) itself bars suit (and thus any damages) for older acts without adding any remedial limitation. TRW and Rotkiske, which Justice Gorsuch also invokes, reinforce that we should not infer a discovery rule from statutory silence; once accrual is fixed at infringement, Petrella’s “three years back” description is simply the statute’s operation, not judicial supplementation. Even accepting the Chief Justice’s minimalist posture arguendo, that premise cannot justify expanding substantive liability for time-barred acts beyond what the text, properly read, permits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest textual point: § 507(b) speaks in terms of when an action must be “commenced,” not an express remedial ceiling. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Petrella’s repeated explanation that the Act “takes account of delay” by limiting retrospective relief to “three years back” was integral to rejecting laches; treating that as disposable dicta would destabilize Petrella’s logic and invite precisely the open-ended, stale-claim exposure limitations provisions are meant to prevent. Even assuming discovery accrual for timeliness, reading § 507(b) to permit boundless backward damages would, in practical effect, convert a filing rule into an engine for unlimited retrospective liability—an implausible consequence absent clear congressional direction, consistent with the caution reflected in TRW and Rotkiske (as Justice Thomas notes) against expanding liability from silence. Diligence inquiries and equitable tailoring, as Justice Jackson suggests, are too case-specific to substitute for the administrable, statute-linked repose boundary Petrella understood to be doing real work.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh are right that Petrella repeatedly described § 507(b) as limiting “retrospective relief only three years back,” but that language was tethered to Petrella’s separate-accrual framework and its rejection of laches—not a holding that a timely suit (here assumed timely under discovery accrual) carries an additional, judge-made remedial forfeiture for older proven harms. Justice Thomas’s TRW/Rotkiske point counsels restraint about implying a discovery rule in the first place, yet it does not justify a second step of reading an uncodified damages cap into § 507(b) once timeliness is conceded; Congress wrote a commencement rule, and the remedial provisions in §§ 502–505 contain no comparable temporal truncation. The repose and staleness concerns emphasized by Justice Alito can be addressed through the diligence component of discovery accrual, evidentiary burdens, and equitable tailoring, without effectively hollowing out discovery accrual for concealed infringement in a way that predictably disadvantages less-resourced creators. On my pragmatic approach, petitioners’ administrable line is appealing but not textually grounded enough to override the statute’s structure and the real-world impact of denying meaningful compensation where the infringement could not reasonably be detected.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Petrella repeatedly spoke of “retrospective relief only three years back” as the statute’s built-in answer to delay, but that statement was made in a separate-accrual, anti-laches setting and cannot supply a free-standing remedial cap that § 507(b) does not textually enact. Textually, § 507(b) tells us when an action must be “commenced” after a claim “accrued”; it does not speak in the remedial terms Congress used elsewhere (e.g., §§ 502–505), so converting it into a categorical damages forfeiture rewrites the statute rather than interprets it. Justice Thomas’s TRW/Rotkiske caution about implying discovery accrual is a serious separation-of-powers point, but once we assume (as the posture here does) that discovery accrual governs timeliness, that caution does not justify a second atextual step—imposing an additional monetary lookback limit untethered to enacted words. Pragmatically, Petitioners’ rule would often drain discovery accrual of meaning in concealed-infringement cases, while staleness and repose concerns can be addressed through the diligence component of accrual, proof requirements, and equitable tailoring without inventing a damages cap.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is textual: § 507(b) speaks in filing terms (“commenced within three years after the claim accrued”) and does not expressly cabin remedies, so a categorical damages lookback can sound like we are adding words. But Petrella—emphasized by the Chief Justice—did not merely observe a timing rule; it identified the statute’s built-in substitute for laches by repeatedly describing the Act as limiting retrospective relief to three years, and that rationale collapses if discovery-based accrual can simultaneously permit unlimited backward monetary exposure. TRW and Rotkiske, as Justice Thomas notes, counsel against using statutory silence to expand liability, and a three-year lookback is the more text-anchored, administrable way to preserve § 507(b)’s repose function while assuming arguendo discovery for timeliness. Justice Jackson’s suggestion of case-by-case proof burdens and equitable tailoring is not a stable substitute for the statute-linked boundary Petrella understood Congress to have supplied.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the hardest point: § 507(b) is cast as a commencement deadline and does not expressly cap remedies, so a categorical three-year lookback can sound atextual. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Petrella’s repeated explanation that the Act “takes account of delay” by confining retrospective relief to three years was integral to rejecting laches; if discovery accrual makes filing timely whenever discovered and simultaneously allows unlimited backward damages, the statute’s repose function—and Petrella’s logic—largely collapses. TRW and Rotkiske, as Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, reinforce the institutional caution against reading silence in limitations language to expand exposure; the administrable, precedent-aligned reconciliation (even assuming discovery for timeliness) is a three-year monetary lookback. Justice Jackson’s proposal to rely on equitable tailoring and proof burdens is important at the margins, but it is too case-specific to substitute for the clear temporal boundary Petrella treated as built into the statutory scheme.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is the textual one: § 507(b) is cast as a commencement rule and does not expressly announce a remedies cap, so a three-year damages lookback can sound like adding words Congress did not write. But Chief Justice Roberts persuasively explains that Petrella’s repeated “retrospective relief only three years back” formulation was integral to the Court’s rejection of laches because it identified the statute’s built-in method of accounting for delay; treating that premise as detachable dicta would destabilize Petrella’s logic and reintroduce the stale-claim concerns laches was invoked to address. TRW and Rotkiske, emphasized by Justices Thomas and Gorsuch, further counsel against using statutory silence in a limitations provision to enlarge monetary exposure, and a three-year lookback is the most administrable way to preserve the repose function while assuming arguendo a discovery-based timeliness rule. Justice Jackson’s suggestion that proof burdens and equitable tailoring can do the work is too case-specific to substitute for the clear temporal boundary Petrella understood the Act to supply.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take seriously Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Petrella’s “three years back” language and their concern that discovery accrual plus full damages would dilute repose, but Petrella’s statements functioned in a separate-accrual/laches posture and do not supply statutory text for a categorical remedial forfeiture in a timely filed action. Section 507(b) is written as a commencement rule (“commenced within three years after the claim accrued”), and adding an across-the-board damages lookback reads a second limitation into silence, effectively relocating Congress’s timeliness choice into a judge-made remedies cap absent from §§ 502–505. Justice Thomas’s TRW/Rotkiske point is a real caution about implying discovery accrual, yet once we assume discovery accrual for timeliness in this case, those precedents do not justify the additional atextual step of curtailing remedies beyond what the Act provides. Administrability and staleness (raised by Justice Alito and Justice Gorsuch) can be handled through the diligence component of discovery accrual, evidentiary burdens, and equitable tailoring rather than a rigid rule that can make timely suits practically worthless in concealed-infringement scenarios.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 507(b) requires an action be “commenced within three years after the claim accrued,” and in Petrella v. MGM the Court emphasized that the Act “itself takes account of delay” by limiting retrospective monetary relief to a three-year lookback window, describing § 507(b) as operating like a limitations period on backward-looking recovery. Allowing discovery-based accrual to open damages for infringements far outside that three-year window would undercut repose and evidentiary reliability and create open-ended liability inconsistent with limitations principles the Court has favored in TRW Inc. v. Andrews and Rotkiske v. Klemm (treating discovery as a narrow exception absent clear statutory direction). A narrow holding enforcing a three-year cap on monetary relief, even assuming discovery accrual for timeliness, best preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to Petrella’s construction and avoiding a broad reshaping of accrual doctrine. Federalism and uniformity concerns also counsel applying a clear, administrable federal remedial boundary rather than leaving the scope of retrospective recovery to variable equitable doctrines.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 507(b) provides that a civil action must be “commenced within three years after the claim accrued,” and the most natural textual reading—consistent with ordinary accrual principles—is that a claim accrues when the infringing act occurs, not upon later discovery absent clear statutory language. In Petrella v. MGM, 572 U.S. 663 (2014), the Court described § 507(b) as a “three-year look-back limitations period” and explained that a suit is timely only as to infringing acts within that three-year window, which necessarily bars monetary recovery for earlier acts. Allowing discovery accrual to resurrect damages for long-past infringements would undermine repose and effectively rewrite § 507(b) into an open-ended damages regime, contrary to this Court’s skepticism of implied discovery rules in TRW Inc. v. Andrews, 534 U.S. 19 (2001), and Rotkiske v. Klemm, 589 U.S. 8 (2019). The statute’s plain text contains no separate authorization for retroactive monetary recovery beyond the limitations period, and precedent should not be extended to create it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 507(b) provides that civil actions must be “commenced within three years after the claim accrued,” and that limitations function is best understood to bar monetary recovery for infringements occurring more than three years before suit, even if a discovery-accrual rule makes the action timely as to later-discovered infringements. In Petrella v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, Inc., this Court repeatedly described § 507(b) as permitting “retrospective relief running only three years back from the date the complaint was filed” and insulating infringers from liability for earlier infringements, language that reflects a practical and repose-protecting cap on backward-looking damages. Allowing open-ended damages whenever discovery is delayed would undermine the statute’s evident purpose of repose and exacerbate evidentiary unreliability, inviting precisely the kind of stale-claim litigation limitations periods are designed to prevent. Consistent with Petrella and the ordinary operation of limitations statutes, I would hold § 507(b) bars monetary relief for infringement acts outside the three-year lookback period.
